analysis.one_liner: Limits fees and notice abuses when debt collectors chase money owed to the federal government.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee without a single no vote but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill extends federal debt-collection consumer protections to money people owe federal agencies, such as overpayments, fines, and fees. It stops agencies from handing a debt to a private collector until 90 days after default, requires three advance notices before a debt is sold or transferred, and bars collectors from charging fees that are excessive, not in their contract, or above 10% of what they collect. It also orders a Government Accountability Office study of how federal, state, and local governments use private debt collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who fall behind on money owed to a federal agency, such as student loan overpayments, fines, or fees, and who currently face private collectors adding interest, fees, and charges on top of the original debt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People owing money to federal agencies

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to cover collections of debts originally owed to federal agencies, a category of debt the law previously did not clearly reach.

Bars a federal agency from selling or transferring a debt to a private collector until 90 days after the debt becomes delinquent or defaults, and requires the agency to notify the consumer three times, spaced at least 30 days apart, before doing so.

Stops collectors of federal-agency debt from charging any interest, fee, or expense that is unreasonable relative to actual collection costs, not authorized by their contract with the agency, or greater than 10% of the amount collected.

Requires the Government Accountability Office to study and report on how federal, state, and local government agencies use private debt collectors, including the fees charged to debtors, revenue-sharing agreements, and whether these collectors are subject to consumer protections.

analysis.who_pays: Private debt collection companies and debt buyers, which would face new limits on the fees and charges they can add when collecting government debt, plus the paper-trail cost of notice requirements for agencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private debt collection firms and debt buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill's core protections apply only to federal-agency debts at least 180 days past due; state and local government debt collection, a major source of collector fees against consumers, is only studied, not regulated.

New restrictions could make it harder or slower for agencies to recover unpaid federal debts, which may shift some of that cost to taxpayers through higher agency administrative expense or lower recovery rates.
Even after the bill's limits, a collector could still lawfully add fees equal to 10% of everything collected, a substantial add-on for consumers already behind on a debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are modest but real: they reach a specific corner of debt collection, government debt, and directly cap the fees collectors can pile on people who are already struggling. The main honest criticism is narrowness, since state and local debt collection is only studied and the federal rules kick in only after 180 days of delinquency. The taxpayer-cost objection is speculative and small relative to the protections gained.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it unanimously and reported it in December 2020, three weeks before the Congress ended, but the House never brought it up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Missouri Democrat, and Rep. French Hill, an Arkansas Republican, introduced the bill together in September 2019.
The House Financial Services Committee considered the bill in markup in November 2019 and ordered it reported, as amended, by a vote of 54 to 0 with no opposition.
The committee formally reported the bill on December 15, 2020, with a report number and placed it on the Union Calendar, where bills wait for a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection firms that collect government debt are better off: they avoided new caps on the fees and charges they can add to consumers' bills, and consumers who owe federal debts keep facing the same add-on fees. The bill had no organized opposition, so no one had to defeat it; it simply never came up for a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors who avoided new fee limits

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican, and the committee reported it by 54-0 with no dissenting votes from either party.

industries.note: These firms collect debts on behalf of federal agencies and profit from interest, fees, and charges added on top of the principal. The bill caps those add-ons at 10% of the amount collected and requires that they reflect actual costs and contract terms.

The bill amends the definition of debt collector to explicitly cover debts obtained by assignment or transfer from another, closing an argument that firms buying old debts were outside the law's scope.

Agencies would face new notice duties and a 90-day waiting period before outsourcing a debt, but would also benefit from clearer rules governing the collectors they hire. The bill does not eliminate agency use of private collectors.
